```{r}

m_all <- glm(f_all, data = dev, family = binomial)
x_all <- model.matrix(f_all, dev)[, -1]; y <- dev$diabetes
```

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 3: the all-markers model is **overfitted** (bootstrap slope 0.80)
- Today: ways to **reduce overfitting**
  - **variable selection**: does it work?
  - **penalised regression** (ridge, lasso)
  - **uniform shrinkage**
:::

# Topic 1 — Variable selection {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Backward stepwise (AIC)

```{r}
m_step <- step(m_all, direction = "backward", trace = 0)
names(coef(m_step))[-1]
```

::: {.warn}
The selection kept **age, waist, family history, hypertension, activity, smoking** (BMI and sex were dropped) **and four noise markers: m6, m8, m9, m10**. With 84 events, selection **chases chance**.
:::

## How stable is the selection?

```{r}
set.seed(3)
sel <- replicate(50, { i <- sample(nrow(dev), replace = TRUE); f <- suppressWarnings(step(glm(f_all, data = dev[i, ], family = binomial), direction = "backward", trace = 0)); paste0("m", 1:10) %in% names(coef(f)) })
round(setNames(rowMeans(sel), paste0("m", 1:10)), 2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Bootstrap inclusion frequency**: every noise marker is selected **12% to 82%** of the time (m10 82%, m9 70%)
- The chosen set **changes with the sample**; **coefficients of selected variables are biased away from zero**; **p-values after selection are not valid**
- **Do not** select by univariable p-values either
- Prefer: **pre-specify** predictors (clinical knowledge, literature), **penalise**, or accept **shrinkage**
:::

# Topic 2 — Penalised regression {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Ridge

```{r}
set.seed(1)
cv_r <- cv.glmnet(x_all, y, family = "binomial", alpha = 0)
round(cbind(ML = coef(m_all)[paste0("m", 1:10)], ridge = as.numeric(coef(cv_r, s = "lambda.min"))[-1][match(paste0("m", 1:10), colnames(x_all))]), 3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Ridge** adds a **penalty on the size of the coefficients** (λ × sum of squares)
- **λ is chosen by cross-validation** (`cv.glmnet`; here λ = 0.036)
- All coefficients **shrink towards zero** (to about **60 to 70%** of the ML values), **none becomes exactly zero**
- **Standardise** the predictors (glmnet does it by default)
:::

## Lasso

```{r}
set.seed(1)
cv_l <- cv.glmnet(x_all, y, family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
b_l <- coef(cv_l, s = "lambda.1se")
rownames(b_l)[as.numeric(b_l) != 0][-1]
```

::: {.key}
The **lasso** (penalty on the **sum of absolute values**) sets some coefficients **exactly to zero**: it **selects and shrinks**. At **λ.1se** (largest penalty within one SE of the best) it kept **only age, waist and family history**: it removed all the **noise markers**, but also the real **hypertension, smoking and activity**: a sparse, probably **over-shrunk** model. `lambda.min` keeps more.
:::

## Uniform shrinkage

```{r}
lp0 <- predict(m_all, dev)
lp_s <- 0.80 * lp0
b0 <- coef(glm(diabetes ~ offset(lp_s), data = dev, family = binomial))[[1]]
c(mean_predicted_after = mean(plogis(lp_s + b0)), prevalence = mean(dev$diabetes)) |> round(3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- Multiply **all coefficients** by the **bootstrap slope (0.80)**, then **re-estimate the intercept** so that the mean risk equals the prevalence
- Predicted risks become **less extreme**; the **ranking (AUC) does not change**
- Simple, transparent, and works with **any** model; the same idea as **ridge**, with one factor
:::

## What to use?

::: {.good}
1. **Pre-specify** a small set of predictors; avoid data-driven selection when events are few
2. If you must reduce, use **penalisation** (ridge for prediction; lasso for sparse models)
3. Always **bootstrap the whole process** (including λ selection and selection steps)
4. Apply **shrinkage** when the bootstrap slope is below about 0.9
5. **External validation** (Session 5) tells you whether it worked
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p4q1", "Backward stepwise selection kept four noise markers. What is the main lesson?",
         c("The markers are real predictors that were missing from the study design plan",
           "Stepwise selection removes noise variables, but it fails with the real ones",
           "Selection follows chance in small samples, and the set varies by sample",
           "Backward selection works if forward selection has been applied first"), answer = 3,
         explain = "With few events per variable, selection follows random patterns, and different samples give different models, as the bootstrap inclusion frequencies show.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p4q2", "What does ridge regression do to the coefficients?",
         c("It sets small coefficients to exactly zero and keeps the large ones unchanged",
           "It increases the largest coefficients to improve discrimination",
           "It removes correlated predictors from the model before fitting",
           "It shrinks all coefficients towards zero without setting them exactly to zero"), answer = 4,
         explain = "The ridge penalty is on the squares of the coefficients, so all of them are pulled towards zero by an amount that depends on lambda.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p4q3", "How is the penalty lambda usually chosen in glmnet?",
         c("By cross-validation, taking the value with the best out-of-sample fit",
           "By the analyst, who picks the value that gives the best apparent AUC value",
           "By the p-value of each coefficient in the unpenalised version of the model",
           "It is fixed at the value 1 for all datasets and need not be chosen at all"), answer = 1,
         explain = "cv.glmnet fits the penalised model over a grid of lambda values and evaluates each by cross-validation. The apparent AUC would favour no penalty at all.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p4q4", "The lasso at lambda.1se kept only age, waist and family history. What does this illustrate?",
         c("Those three are the variables that are really related to diabetes in the data",
           "It can remove noise, but also real predictors when the penalty is large",
           "The lasso keeps variables in the order of their p-values in the full model",
           "Variables with a low prevalence cannot be selected by the lasso procedure"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A strong penalty sets many coefficients to zero, including real ones. Choosing lambda.min or checking external calibration shows whether the model is over-shrunk.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p4q5", "What is uniform shrinkage?",
         c("Dividing the dataset into equal parts and fitting a separate model in each",
           "Setting every coefficient to the average of the coefficients of the model",
           "Rounding all coefficients to the nearest whole number for use as a score",
           "Multiplying coefficients by a factor below 1 and refitting the intercept"), answer = 4,
         explain = "A single factor, often the bootstrap calibration slope, pulls all coefficients towards zero. The intercept is refitted so that the average risk stays correct.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **Stepwise** selection is **unstable**: noise markers chosen, biased coefficients
- **Ridge** shrinks all; **lasso** shrinks and selects
- **λ by cross-validation**; standardise predictors
- **Uniform shrinkage** = bootstrap slope × coefficients, new intercept
- Pre-specify predictors; **validate externally**
:::
